input: This memo provides a recommendation in relation to the proposed deployment of condition-monitoring sensors across the plant's pump fleet, with a view to reducing unplanned downtime and improving overall maintenance performance going forward. The plant currently operates 260 pumps, and a review of the maintenance records covering the last 12 months shows a total of 928 h of unplanned downtime, with bearing failures accounting for 39% of the downtime hours. A sensor set covering all 260 pumps has been quoted at $439k installed, together with a recurring cost of $58k per year. In a vendor trial carried out on a comparable unit, the sensors were able to cut downtime by 22%, although it should be noted that this figure is a vendor figure and was not measured at this plant. Rather than proceeding directly to a full installation, it is recommended that a pilot be conducted on 20 pumps at a cost of $37k over a period of three months. The reliability engineering group owns the pilot and will report before the March capital review, and the decision on full installation is held until the pilot results are reported. It is also worth noting that spare-part lead times are unchanged by the sensors, so this aspect of maintenance performance would not be expected to change as a result of the project. Overall, the pilot represents a measured, low-risk step that will generate plant-specific evidence in support of the subsequent investment decision, helping to ensure that any future commitment of capital is based on robust, locally validated data rather than on vendor claims alone. By taking this staged approach, the plant can leverage the available evidence while minimising exposure, and the findings of the pilot will inform the wider reliability strategy in due course.
target:
The reliability engineering group recommends a three-month pilot of condition sensors on 20 pumps, at a cost of $37k, before any decision on full installation. The group owns the pilot and reports before the March capital review; the decision on full installation is held until the pilot results are reported.

The plant runs 260 pumps. Maintenance records for 12 months show 928 h of unplanned downtime, and bearing failures account for 39% of the downtime hours. The downtime is concentrated in one failure mode, and bearing condition is what a sensor set monitors, so the proposed measure addresses the largest recorded source of lost hours directly. A sensor set for all 260 pumps is quoted at $439k installed, plus $58k per year. In a vendor trial on a comparable unit, the sensors cut downtime by 22%. That figure is a vendor figure and was not measured at this plant; no reduction measured on this plant's pumps exists yet. Spare-part lead times are unchanged by the sensors, so the case for installation rests on downtime alone and on nothing else the sensors might improve.

The pilot is the step that replaces the vendor figure with plant data. Twenty pumps under monitoring for three months give the reliability engineering group a measured reduction, or the absence of one, on the equipment the full installation would cover. The March capital review then decides on full installation with the pilot results in front of it, rather than on a trial run elsewhere. The pilot also bounds the exposure: the expenditure under test is the pilot cost, and the larger commitment is made only after the plant has its own downtime figures for monitored and unmonitored pumps working side by side.
